note: Read by scripts/route.mjs. Each signal is a regular expression (case-insensitive) with a weight. The stack with the highest total wins; ties go to the stack listed first. Edit this file to teach the router a new phrase, then run tests/route.test.mjs. The "patterns" list maps motion phrases to the recipe pages in references/patterns/; each pattern carries example phrases that tests/route.test.mjs must route back to it.

stacks.name: Canvas/WebGL particles (the dust engine)
stacks.why: The brief wants dots or dust that form a picture, a face, a logo or a word. That is the built-in engine: config only, no new code.

stacks.name: React Three Fiber and drei
stacks.why: The brief wants real 3D inside a React or Next.js project, so the scene should be components (React Three Fiber) with drei helpers, built by the project's bundler.

stacks.name: three.js
stacks.why: The brief wants a real 3D object or scene: something to turn, light and look around. Plain three.js needs no build step and is the lightest way to get there.

stacks.name: Motion for React
stacks.why: The project is React or Next.js and the motion belongs to the interface: layout changes, lists, presence, drag, springs. Motion for React expresses those as props on components.

stacks.name: GSAP with ScrollTrigger and Lenis
stacks.why: The brief describes a sequence tied to scrolling: pinned sections, scrubbed timelines, sideways galleries or a picture sequence. GSAP timelines with ScrollTrigger are the dependable tool for that, with Lenis for smooth scroll.

stacks.name: View Transitions API
stacks.why: The brief is about moving between pages or states: a thumbnail that grows into the next page, a grid that reorders. The browser's View Transitions API does this with almost no script and falls back to an ordinary page change.
signals: \b(page transitions?|view transitions?|between pages|page to page|route transitions?|shared element)\b

stacks.name: Lottie and Rive players
stacks.why: The animation already exists as a file from a designer (a Lottie JSON or a Rive file), or the brief wants character-style illustration that is easier to author in a tool than in code. The page's job is to load and play it well.

stacks.name: SVG and CSS animation
stacks.why: The brief is about lines, shapes, icons or charts that draw and change. SVG with the Web Animations API or CSS does that sharply at any size, with no library, or with D3 for scales when there is data.

stacks.name: Motion (vanilla JavaScript)
stacks.why: The brief is led by type and interface feel on a plain page: headlines that set themselves, springs, scroll-linked values. Motion's small JavaScript API does that with hardware-accelerated animations and no framework.
signals: \b(kinetic (type|typography|text)|type animation|text animation|split text|word by word|letter by letter|headline animat\w+|marquee)\b

stacks.name: Plain CSS and JavaScript (the kit)
stacks.why: Nothing in the brief needs a library. CSS transitions, the Web Animations API, IntersectionObserver and native scroll-driven animation cover it, with the kit's helpers for the parts that are easy to get wrong. This is the default: it is the lightest and has nothing to break.

supporting.why: the brief has a headline or words that move
signals: \b(kinetic|headline|word by word|letter by letter|split text|type animation|text animation|marquee|typograph\w+)\b

audiences.why: hardware sells on the object itself: a quiet page, one large product, little else
money and law need trust and fast scanning: a strict grid, high contrast and almost no decoration
health audiences include people who are stressed or have low vision: calm, plain and high contrast
a young audience responds to soft, toy-like shapes and bright colour
developers work in dark editors and want density and directness; a dark default is expected here
an abstract product with no photo to show: soft gradients carry the mood while plain type carries the claim
luxury reads through restraint, large serif type and a lot of space
music brands sell energy: dense colour, big type and treated photography
gaming audiences expect a dark, lit, high-energy look
fashion follows magazine layout, or pushes against it on purpose
independent products win by having a voice: bold outlines and flat colour are quick to recognise
reading comes first: a type scale, a measure and a grid
the work is the content: a quiet grid keeps attention on it
craft and food want warmth and a printed, tactile feel
a product with several features to show at a glance: tiles, one accent and plain type
when the content is pictures, controls should float lightly above it
systems are easier to explain as small models seen from above
an Android product should feel native to its platform

moods.why: the brief asks for a future look
the brief asks for a past decade

Hero animation: the headline sets itself, then the button.

patterns.name: Text line reveal

examples: Words light up one by one as you scroll through our manifesto.
The paragraph reads itself as it crosses the screen.

patterns.name: Marquee
